nodes.name: Failure
nodes.notes:
Fires on a PRODUCTION execution failure in any workflow that names this one as
its error workflow. It does NOT fire on a manual "Test workflow" run, which is a
trap worth knowing: a hand-tested failure looks like the handler is broken when
it simply was not called.

nodes.name: Count Attempts
nodes.notes:
A transient error inside its retry budget is recorded and stays quiet; the same
error three times running is no longer transient and does alert. Alert fatigue is
not a minor annoyance - an operator who has learned to ignore this mailbox is the
same as having no alerting at all.

nodes.name: Write Audit Row

value.detail_json: ={{ JSON.stringify({ node: $json.node_name, error: $json.error, severity: $json.severity, attempts: $json.attempts, execution_url: $json.execution_url }) }}

nodes.notes:
The dead-letter table is state ("what is still broken"); the audit table is
history ("what happened, in order"). Resolving a dead letter changes its state
row; it must not erase the fact that the failure occurred.

Named "Write Audit Row" and not "Write Error Audit" for a mechanical reason:
n8n's validator infers a node's ROLE from its name, and flagged the old name as
an error handler wrongly wired onto a success output. It is an ordinary write on
one of three parallel branches. Renaming it was cheaper than teaching every
future reader to ignore a red error in the validation report.

nodes.name: Send Alert Email
nodes.notes:
continueErrorOutput, not continueRegularOutput. The difference matters: this
routes a failed send down a SECOND branch that records it, instead of letting the
flow carry on as though the alert went out.

The failure mode being defended against is specific and has happened here: the
Gmail credential itself expires, so the one channel that would tell you a
credential died is the credential that died. Production wants a second channel on
a different credential (Telegram, Slack, PagerDuty) - one node, wired to the same
error output. It is deliberately not wired here because it would bind this repo
to a private bot token that no reviewer can run.

nodes.name: Replay Request
nodes.notes:
POST { "dlq_id": "dlq-...", "override_json": "{...}" }

override_json is how a quarantined CSV row is fixed and resubmitted: correct the
field, replay the dead letter. Without it the operator would have to rebuild the
original request by hand from a log line.

nodes.name: Read Lead Ledger
nodes.notes:
Every claim ever made for this lead, across every scope. This read is what makes
a replay safe rather than hopeful - it is the difference between "run it again and
see" and "run only the parts that never finished".

nodes.name: Respond Replay
nodes.notes:
The status code carries the outcome (404 unknown id, 409 already handled, 422
nothing to replay, 202 accepted) and the body says which steps were skipped and
why, so an operator can see that the replay respected the completed work rather
than having to go and check Odoo.

nodes.name: Mark Dead Letter Replayed
nodes.notes:
State moves to "replayed", never to deleted. A dead letter is evidence: what
failed, how often, and what was done about it. Deleting it on success throws away
the only record that the incident happened.

first_seen is written as 0 because upsert rewrites the whole row and the original
value is preserved in the audit history instead - a documented limitation of the
Data Table node, which has no partial update.

parameters.content:
## LP-05 Error Handler and DLQ

**Capture** (top): every workflow names this one as its `errorWorkflow`. Failures are classified `transient` / `credential` / `permanent`, dead-lettered under a stable id so a repeat increments instead of multiplying, and alerted **only when a human can act** - a transient inside its retry budget stays quiet, a dead credential is critical on sight.

**Replay** (bottom): `POST /webhook/lp-replay {"dlq_id":"..."}`. It reads the idempotency ledger **before** doing anything, so a re-run after a partial success skips the steps that already completed and cannot create a second Odoo opportunity. **(EC-14)**

**This workflow has no error workflow of its own** - that would loop. Every node here is written to survive its own failure, and the alert path degrades to a `critical` audit row.
